title: Going to your brother (Matthew 18:15–17)
hookLine: Jesus' steps for a wrong between people: speak privately first, aiming to win the person back

cards: Someone close does something that stings. A comment in front of others. A promise quietly dropped.
There are two easy moves. One is to tell everyone else: a friend, a sibling, a group chat, anyone except the person who did it. The other is to say nothing and let it sour slowly.
Jesus offers a third move, and it may be the hardest of the three, because it goes straight to the one person you'd rather avoid.
Yesterday's line still stands: this is for ordinary hurts between people who are safe with each other.

teach.b: In Matthew 18, Jesus lays out steps, and the order matters.
Step one, in the King James Bible: "if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." Alone.
Before anyone else hears about it. And the goal: gained thy brother.

teach.h: ONE OR TWO MORE, FOR FAIRNESS.
teach.b: Not won the argument; won back the person. Step two, only if step one fails: take one or two others along, "that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established."
That phrase comes from the Torah's own rule for fair judgment, in Deuteronomy. The witnesses aren't there to gang up. They're there to keep things fair and clear.
Step three: "tell it unto the church."
And if he won't hear even the church, Jesus says, "let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican." Here readers part ways.
Some churches read this as a step of formal discipline: the person is treated as outside the fellowship until they turn back. Other readers notice who is telling the story.
The Gospel itself calls its namesake Matthew the publican, a tax collector, and Jesus ate with tax collectors. So they hear it as: start over with them, the way Jesus started with Matthew.
Either way, the shape is the same. The circle begins at its smallest. The hope is that it never has to widen.
Going privately protects the other person's dignity, and it gives the friendship a real chance.

how: Christians use Matthew 18:15–17 as a guide for conflict in families, friendships and congregations; some churches build it into their rules for church discipline, and pastors coach members to go to the person privately before involving anyone else.

games.q: what does “going to your brother” mean?
o: telling someone their wrong privately, to win them back
asking a family member to settle a quarrel for you
reporting a wrong to church leaders straight away

s: Jesus' first step is to tell the whole church
the first step is "between thee and him alone." the church comes last.
the aim of step one is to win the person back
"if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."
the witnesses in step two are there to outnumber the other person
the phrase about two or three witnesses comes from the Torah's rule for fair judgment: they keep things fair and clear.

games.q: a close friend embarrassed you in front of others, and it still stings. by Jesus' steps in Matthew 18, what comes first?
o: tell a few trusted people what happened.
go to the friend alone and tell them.
bring two witnesses and confront them.
games.why: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone." witnesses come only if that fails, and the church only after that.

practice: Bring to mind one hurt from someone you're close to that you've told others about, or swallowed, and picture going to them alone.

Find your first sentence, plain and short, what happened and how it landed on you, with no list of old grievances, and say it silently a few times until it sounds like you. If you pray, you can ask for a soft voice and a fair ear.

wordCard.voice: Going to your brother. Jesus' first step when someone wrongs you: tell them alone, hoping to win them back.

orig.note: Greek: you have gained, from a verb for making a profit; "thou hast gained thy brother" (Matthew 18:15).

carryVoice: Your line: go privately first. The circle begins at its smallest. Back tomorrow, same hill.
